meta.subtitle: Q1 FY27 10-Q: RPO of $664 billion, the full-year guide raised, and free cash flow still negative

analystCommentary:
Our disagreement with the street is about timing, not about demand.

The demand side is as settled as this filing can settle it. Remaining Performance Obligations rose $209 billion year over year to $664 billion, management said the backlog began converting into revenue during the quarter, and the full-year guide went up on the strength of it. We do not dispute any of that, and the rest of this report does not argue with it.

What contracts do not do is arrive as cash. Oracle is funding delivery out of debt and equity, the reported record shows no year in which that turns, and the capital guide for this year is larger again. A buyer at today's price is underwriting the funding, not the demand.

So we sit well below the $236.52 consensus target, and we hold a BUY rather than a HOLD because the question is when the cash arrives, not whether. A backlog of that size is strong evidence for the revenue side of this thesis and no evidence at all for the cash side, and the cash side is what our discount reflects.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
### What Oracle sells

Oracle provides products and services that build, run and support enterprise information technology frameworks, delivered through cloud-based, on-premise and hybrid deployment models. The 10-Q names three businesses, each comprised of a single operating segment: cloud and software; hardware; and services.

On a trailing four-quarter basis the filing puts cloud and software at 88% of total revenues, hardware at 4% and services at 8%. Inside cloud and software the balance has moved toward cloud, and the financials section sets out by how much.

The quarter's revenue lines show where that mix sits today. Total Cloud Revenues were $11.6 billion, up 62%, split between Cloud Infra (IaaS) at $7.4 billion, up 121%, and Cloud Apps (SaaS) at $4.2 billion, up 10%. Software revenues were down 3% to $5.5 billion, which the release attributes to customers' continuing migration from on-premises software to the Cloud. Services revenues were $1.4 billion, up 5%, and Hardware revenues were $0.8 billion, up 15%.

The cloud and software portfolio spans the Oracle Fusion Cloud suite covering ERP, EPM, SCM and HCM, the NetSuite application suite, Oracle Database, Oracle Middleware and Java, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure compute, storage and networking. Hardware covers Oracle Engineered Systems, servers, storage and the related hardware software, sold mostly through independent distributors and value-added resellers. Services is consulting services and customer success services, which the filing states carries lower margins than the other two businesses.

Revenue is concentrated in the Americas at 63.3% of the FY25 geographic mix, with EMEA at 24.4% and Asia Pacific at 12.3%. Oracle was established in 1977 and is headquartered in Austin, Texas.

thesis.body:
Oracle is converting a contracted backlog into revenue at speed, and funding the conversion well ahead of the cash it produces.

The backlog now has a published size. Remaining Performance Obligations reached $664 billion, and management expects around half of that to convert into sales over the next 36 months. The conversion has physical evidence behind it: 850 megawatts of capacity delivered since the end of Q4, and cloud infrastructure revenue of $7.4 billion in the quarter, up 121%.

The funding gap is in the tables. Capital expenditure was {- -$55.7B -} in FY26 against {- -$21.2B -} in FY25, free cash flow was {- -$23.7B -} on operating cash flow of $32.0B, and total debt rose to $156.2B from $104.1B. The leverage and the coverage that result are argued in the balance sheet section.

Our base case is that the revenue arrives roughly on the guided path while the cash return arrives later than the consensus target assumes. The distribution is wide on both sides, and the bear case here is a funding case, not a demand case.

catalysts: **Conversion has begun.** Part of the backlog turned into reported revenue this quarter on management's own account, and the growth section says what it drove.

**The full-year guide went up on this call.** Management raised both the revenue and the non-GAAP EPS lines for fiscal 2027, which is the part of the backlog story a reader can check within three quarters.
**Capacity is landing, not just contracted.** Oracle delivered almost three times the Q4 volume in Q1, and delivered capacity, unlike contracted backlog, converts into revenue.

**Renewals priced up, not down.** Management said GPUs coming up for renewal in Q1 were renewed or resold at a 20% premium to prior contracts, on a cohort the majority of which is four years or older.
**Multicloud is compounding.** Multicloud database revenue grew 353% year over year, across a regional footprint Oracle completed inside the quarter.
**Contracts are arriving customer-funded.** The release states that, based on the structuring of the new contracts, the Company confirms there is no incremental impact on its plans to raise capital.
risks: **The capital line has stepped up twice in two years.** Each of the last two fiscal years multiplied the prior year's capital expenditure, and FY27 is guided higher again.
**Free cash flow is negative and debt is funding the gap.** FY26 free cash flow was negative and total debt rose to fund it; on a trailing basis the FCF yield is {- -6.6% -}.
**Interest is now a claim on operating profit.** The build was financed, so a share of operating profit is committed before any of it reaches the equity.

**Gross margin falls as infrastructure mix rises.** The annual ratio declined in each of the four years since FY22, and management ties the quarter's decline to the data center ramp and the infrastructure mix, while the multi-year fall carries no explanation in the sources.

**The software line is falling.** Software revenues, license and support together, fell 3% in the quarter while cloud infrastructure grew at triple digits; no split between the two exists here, so the direction of the support annuity itself is not visible.
**The fleet is running full.** GPU utilization of 97.9% leaves no spare capacity, and the risks section carries what that implies for capital.

financials.incomeCommentary:
### The quarter, and the year behind it

The 10-Q covers the three months ended August 31, 2026. Revenue was $19.3B, {+ +29.6% +} year over year, at a 35.3% operating margin against a trailing twelve month operating margin of 32.5%. The mix inside that is the story: the filing puts cloud revenues at 60% of total revenues for the quarter, where the same three months a year earlier came in at 48%.

Both bases are now on the table, and they differ. GAAP operating income was $6.7 billion, up 57%, and GAAP earnings per share $1.56, up 55%. The figures management leads with are non-GAAP: operating income of $8.2 billion, up 31%, at a margin it described as around flat at 42%, and earnings per share of $1.92. The bridge between the two is $1,423 million of stock-based compensation, amortization of intangible assets and restructuring, all removed from operating expenses.

The five-year series gives the context. FY26 revenue was $67.4B, {+ +17.4% +}, ahead of the +8.4% of FY25 and the +6.0% of FY24 but a shade below the +17.7% Oracle posted in FY23. Operating income was $20.8B against $17.7B, EBITDA $32.1B against $23.9B, net income $17.1B against $12.4B, and diluted EPS $5.83 against $4.34.

The build shows up in margin. Gross margin was 65.2% in FY26 against 70.5% in FY25 and 79.1% in FY22. Operating income rose while gross margin fell by more than five points, so operating expenses came down as a share of revenue and the operating margin held roughly flat. Nothing in the sources explains why the annual ratio moved that way. For the quarter management does explain it, attributing the decline to ramping up data centers and the acceleration of infrastructure revenue, offset by lower operating costs and operating leverage. One conflict is worth stating once: the trailing twelve month gross margin of 74.4% does not reconcile with the FY26 statement figure above, and we have used the statement series throughout this report.

Guidance changed on this call. The full-year revenue outlook went up, non-GAAP EPS for the year is now guided to $8.10, and the Q2 FY27 range for non-GAAP EPS is $1.85 to $1.93. Management frames that range as 21% to 25% growth once the one-time Ampere gain booked in the year-ago quarter is excluded, and as a decline of 14% to 18% including it.
financials.balanceCommentary:
### The balance sheet behind the build

At FY26 year end Oracle held $31.9B of cash and short-term investments against $11.2B a year earlier, and total debt of $156.2B against $104.1B. Net debt was $124.9B, up from $93.3B in FY25 and from $54.5B in FY22. Total equity moved from -$5.8B in FY22 to $43.1B in FY26, closing the equity deficit of four years earlier, and the current ratio improved to 1.12 from 0.75, with the trailing twelve month reading at 1.17.

The trailing leverage line is the one to hold on to, here and everywhere else in this report. Net debt runs at 3.2x EBITDA and interest coverage at 4.6x. Neither reading is distressed for a company of this size, and neither leaves much room in a build still being funded. Interest expense was $1,428 million in the quarter against $923 million a year earlier.

The equity side changed inside the quarter. Oracle completed the sale of $20 billion of common stock, before commissions, through an At-the-Market equity program. Neither the filing nor the release gives an issue price, so what that dilution cost an existing holder cannot be worked out from these documents. The cover page puts shares outstanding at 3.02B. The income statement also carries $81 million of preferred stock dividends for the quarter against none a year earlier, so common holders now rank behind a preferred claim as well as a larger share count.

The gaps matter as much as the figures. The 10-Q's forward-looking statements section points the reader to Part I, Item 1A of the Form 10-K for the year ended May 31, 2026, and no Item 1A from the quarterly filing reaches us here, so whether the risk disclosure changed cannot be read from what we have. There is no disclosure on debt terms, maturities or covenants either, so none of the judgment above rests on one.
financials.cashflowCommentary:
### The cash statement carries the argument

The cash flow table shows the capital line directly. Capital expenditure ran {- -$4.5B -} in FY22, {- -$8.7B -} in FY23, {- -$6.9B -} in FY24, {- -$21.2B -} in FY25 and {- -$55.7B -} in FY26. Operating cash flow over the same span ran from $9.5B in FY22 to $32.0B in FY26. Operating cash flow grew; capital spending grew faster.

The consequence is two consecutive negative years. Free cash flow was a positive $11.8B in FY24, then {- -$0.4B -} in FY25 and {- -$23.7B -} in FY26, an FCF margin of {- -35.2% -}. The trailing twelve month FCF yield is {- -6.6% -}.

The quarter ran the same way at a better ratio. Oracle reported Q1 operating cash flow of $23 billion, up 184%, and free cash flow of negative $5 billion. Management put CapEx for the quarter at $28 billion and net cash CapEx, after customer prepayments, at $18 billion. It guided the full year to $90 billion-$95 billion of CapEx with not more than $70 billion of net cash CapEx, and noted the spending will not be linear across the year.

Management's position is that the incremental backlog is customer-funded. It said the vast majority of the contracts added in the quarter came via prepay or bring your own hardware or similar mechanic and so will not require incremental capital from Oracle, that Oracle booked more than $30 billion of additional AI cloud contracts in Q1 on that basis, and that this new RPO will not impact CapEx or revenues until fiscal 2028 or beyond. Grant the claim in full and it still describes the contracts signed, not the capacity already being built. The spend guided for this year is unaffected by it, and that spend is what produces this year's deficit.

Asked about the model on the call, management described access to capital and the different ways of funding it as a constraint the industry is adapting to. That is the honest frame. Free cash flow has to turn before the debt compounds into the equity story, and neither FY26 nor this quarter shows the turn.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
### What the price already assumes

Oracle trades at 23.2x trailing earnings, 6.0x sales, 14.7x EV/EBITDA and 18.5x forward NTM earnings. Against FY28E EPS of $11.02 the forward multiple is roughly 13.6x.

Treat that forward figure as an assumption, not as a valuation. A market paying that multiple for earnings two years out is not paying for those earnings. It is paying close to the trailing multiple on results already reported, and discounting the FY28E step to $131.2B of revenue to a fraction of its face value. The raised full-year guide narrows the nearer half of that step, which is the part a reader can check inside a year. It says nothing yet about the far half, and the far half carries the multiple gap.

A backlog of $664 billion set against a market capitalization of ~$432.5B looks like the whole argument for a re-rating until the timing is applied. Management expects around half to convert over the next 36 months and says the newest contracts will not affect revenues until fiscal 2028 or beyond, so most of that figure lands outside the window this report values, and none of it is cash today.

The street has not resolved it either. 86 analysts split Buy 56 · Hold 26 · Sell 4, around a median target of $241.00 and a range running $95.00-$325.00.

Two qualifications on the multiples themselves. The EV/EBITDA figure above rests on an EBITDA base that excludes the depreciation of a capital program still being built, so it flatters a balance sheet carrying $124.9B of net debt. And no peer column exists in this pack, so every multiple here is judged against Oracle's own history alone.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Capacity converts and holds its price. Delivery holds near the pace management reported for Q1, utilization stays close to 97.9%, and renewal pricing holds the 20% premium, so the fleet outlives its depreciation schedule. RPO converts on the schedule management describes, FY28E revenue of $131.2B and EPS of $11.02 are met, prepaid contracts hold net cash CapEx below the guided $70 billion, and free cash flow inflects during fiscal 2028 without a further equity raise. On that record the multiple re-rates past the median street target of $241.00.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: The guided revenue arrives and the cash return lags. The raised outlook of at least $90 billion is met, the FY28E consensus EPS is approached but not reached, and gross margin stays nearer the FY26 level than the FY25 one. Free cash flow stays negative through FY27, and the debt funding it caps the multiple Oracle can earn. The $180 is the level at which a business that delivers its revenue but not its cash should trade: above today's price because the revenue is contracted, and far below what the consensus target implies.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Funding binds before the returns land. Capacity delivery slows or renews at a discount instead of a premium, multicloud growth decelerates from 353%, and the FY28E revenue estimate proves far too high. Further years of negative free cash flow after FY26 force issuance on worse terms, on a balance sheet already carrying the leverage described above. Management's own description of capital access as an industry constraint becomes the binding one, and the equity absorbs the gap.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
### How the band is built

The three cases weight to a fair value of $181.70 against the $150.15 last price. The target band is $165 to $205 and brackets the $180 base case, which carries 48% of the weight. The band is a twelve-month range we would trade around, not a floor under the price.

Bull carries 27%, and that number is a judgment about conjunction rather than about any single condition. The bull case needs delivery to hold its pace, renewals to hold their premium, the FY28E figures to be met in full, net cash CapEx to stay inside the guide, and free cash flow to inflect without a further equity raise. Each is plausible alone. All of them together, on a backlog management says will not reach revenue until fiscal 2028 or beyond, is not a base case.

Bear carries 25%. The central bear mechanism for any GPU-heavy build is that the assets lose value faster than they earn it, and the renewal premium management disclosed for the quarter is the one piece of evidence in front of us bearing directly on that mechanism. It points against the bear, and one quarter of it is not a trend, which is why the weight sits at a quarter of the distribution rather than higher. Our bear price is the bottom of the street's own target range and sits below the 52-week low, so it is a level the market has already been asked to consider, not an invented floor.

Base still carries the heaviest weight. The quarter delivered $19.3B of revenue, {+ +29.6% +}, and the full-year guide went up. But capital expenditure of {- -$55.7B -} in FY26 and a free cash flow line still below zero mean the shareholder is funding the conversion, and no reported figure yet shows the return on that funding.

The bear weight is still heavier than the analyst split implies. Total debt of $156.2B stands against total equity of $43.1B, and a 52-week range of $114.50-$329.50 shows how much multiple this equity can lose inside a year.

segments.name: Cloud And License Business
segments.body:
85.8% of the FY25 revenue mix at $49.2B. The 10-Q calls the business cloud and software and puts it at 88% of total revenues on a trailing four-quarter basis.

Two economics sit inside the one segment. Software support is the durable half: the filing states that substantially all software support customers renew their support contracts with us upon expiration, that those contracts are priced as a percentage of the net fees paid by the customer to purchase a software license, billed in advance, and recognized ratably over a term that is generally one year. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure is the other half, and it is the half that moved: the cloud share of total revenues climbed over the quarter on the mix shift already described, while the software line went the other way.

The filing is explicit that the growing half carries different costs. It names supply chain and energy costs, tariffs and other trade barriers, inflation and currency among the factors that may adversely impact this business' margin. Anyone underwriting the segment today is underwriting the infrastructure economics, not the support annuity.

segments.name: Hardware Business
segments.body:
5.1% of the FY25 revenue mix at $2.9B, and 4% of total revenues on a trailing four-quarter basis per the 10-Q. Hardware revenues were $0.8 billion in the quarter, up 15%. The range covers Oracle Engineered Systems, servers, storage and the operating system, virtualization and management software sold with them, the majority through independent distributors and value-added resellers.

The filing is candid that quarterly hardware revenues are difficult to predict, and names among the causes its manufacturing partners' abilities to timely and cost-effectively manufacture or deliver a few large hardware transactions, customer demand for competing offerings including cloud infrastructure offerings, and the effect of tariffs and other trade barriers on costs. Hardware support is the steadier piece, priced as a percentage of the net hardware products fees and recognized ratably over a term that is generally one year.

At this share the segment does not move the equity. It matters as a trade-policy exposure and as a reminder that Oracle still sits behind a physical supply chain.

segments.name: Services Business
segments.body:
Services took 9.1% of the FY25 revenue mix, or $5.2B; the 10-Q puts the business at 8% of total revenues across the trailing four quarters. Services revenues were $1.4 billion in the quarter, up 5%. The business is consulting services and customer success services, recognized over time as the services are performed.

The filing states that this business has lower margins than the cloud and software and hardware businesses, and that its cost consists primarily of personnel-related expenses, with technology infrastructure, facilities and external contractor expenses alongside. Its revenue is derivative: the 10-Q ties services demand to customer demand for the cloud and software and hardware offerings the services attach to.

Management said that at AI World in October it will unveil an agentic AI accelerator intended to compress SaaS deployments from years to months, and months to weeks. If it works as described it would reduce the implementation hours a customer buys, which would cut into this segment's own revenue. No evidence bearing on that product exists here.

moatFactors.name: Software support renewals
moatFactors.body: The 10-Q states that substantially all software support customers renew their support contracts with us upon expiration, in order to continue to benefit from technical support services and the periodic issuance of unspecified updates and enhancements. Support is priced as a percentage of the net fees paid to purchase a software license, billed in advance of the services being performed, and recognized ratably. That makes it the revenue stream least exposed to the current capital cycle. This pack carries no revenue or margin split by stream, so how much of reported profitability it supplies cannot be sized from what is here.

moatFactors.name: Database and Java installed base
moatFactors.body: The filing names Oracle Applications, Oracle Database, Oracle Middleware and Java among the licensed products, and describes programs that let customers pivot those licenses and the related software support to the Oracle Cloud for new deployments and migrate and expand existing workloads there. The installed base functions as a channel into the cloud, not as a stranded legacy asset, and the migration programs are the mechanism by which it does. The $5.5 billion of software revenue reported for the quarter, down 3%, is what that migration looks like in the reported line.

moatFactors.name: Multicloud database reach
moatFactors.body: Oracle put its database inside competitors' clouds as well as its own. Management reported multicloud database revenue growing 353% year over year and multicloud customers growing 180%, across 70 multicloud database regions and 119 availability zones, and said Oracle Interconnect for AWS is now generally available so OCI has private connections to all hyperscalers with no data transfer charges. The effect is to make the hyperscaler choice less decisive for the database decision, which protects the database rather than the infrastructure.

moatFactors.name: Cloud infrastructure scale
moatFactors.body: Management reported 850 megawatts of AI capacity containing more than 300,000 GPUs delivered since the end of Q4, which it put at 73% of the capacity delivered in all of last fiscal year, at 97.9% GPU utilization. Scale of this kind is bought, not accumulated: it rests on the capital program, and the 10-Q names Oracle's ability to manage Oracle Cloud capacity requirements to meet existing and prospective customer demand as a factor in this business' revenue growth. We treat this as the weakest of the four moat sources even though it is the one the market is paying attention to.

businessMoat.durability:
We rate the moat WIDE, and the rating still rests more on the old business than on the new one. The filing's statement that substantially all software support customers renew, set against a database, middleware and Java base embedded in customer systems, gives Oracle high switching costs and a renewal base independent of the capital program. Renewal at that rate evidences retention; it is not by itself evidence of pricing power, since nothing here shows pricing or churn for that stream.

The infrastructure half is where the moat question is genuinely open, and this filing moved it. A GPU fleet whose renewals priced at a 20% premium, on assets the majority of which are four years or older, is behaving less like a depreciating commodity and more like scarce capacity. Against that, the quarter's cloud growth arrived with the gross margin decline management attributed to ramping data centers.

The summary we would still give is that Oracle is spending an entrenched franchise's cash flow to buy a position in a more contestable business. The renewal premium is evidence that the new position may prove more defensible than we assumed. One quarter of it, reported by management, is not enough to change the rating.

points: **The annual record.** Revenue grew from $42.4B in FY22 to $67.4B in FY26, at +17.7%, +6.0%, +8.4% and {+ +17.4% +}. Two of those four years were single digit and FY26 did not match FY23, so the reacceleration is a return to a prior rate, not a new high.

**What is guided, and what is only estimated.** Management raised the full-year outlook to at least $90 billion of total revenues, +34%, and $8.10 of non-GAAP EPS, and guided Q2 FY27 revenue growth of between 30% and 34% with cloud revenue growth of between 65% and 71%. Consensus for FY28E revenue of $131.2B carries no guidance behind it and remains an estimate.

**Where the growth sits.** Cloud infrastructure revenue was $7.4 billion in the quarter, up 121%, against cloud apps up 10%, and the cloud share of total revenues moves with it. The capital-intensive half is carrying the growth.

**Delivered capacity is now the leading indicator.** Management said Oracle delivered 850 megawatts of AI capacity with more than 300,000 GPUs since the end of Q4, almost three times the Q4 volume, and 131,000 GPUs at Abilene alone, where six of eight campus buildings and 618 megawatts have been delivered to the customer. Delivered capacity converts into revenue; contracted backlog on its own does not.

**Backlog timing.** Remaining Performance Obligations reached $664 billion, up $209 billion year over year and $26 billion from Q4, and Oracle booked more than $30 billion of additional AI cloud contracts in the quarter. Management said it started to see a strong conversion of RPO into revenues this quarter, driving its cloud infrastructure results, and expects around half of the total to convert over the next 36 months.

management.leadership:
### Leadership

The 10-Q identifies the chief operating decision makers as our Chief Executive Officers and Chief Technology Officer, so Oracle runs a co-chief-executive structure with the Chief Technology Officer sharing authority over how resources are allocated across the three businesses. The proxy records the change behind it without naming its result: Ms. Catz retired as CEO and principal financial officer on September 22, 2025 and became Executive Vice Chair, and Mr. Magouyrk and Mr. Sicilia joined the Board as non-independent directors the same day. The excerpt does not name those Chief Executive Officers, so the structure rests on the 10-Q's plural alone. That Chief Technology Officer is Mr. Ellison, the founder, whose stake the ownership section records.

The September call was specific in a way that is useful to an outside reader: hard numbers on delivered capacity, utilization, Abilene and renewal pricing, each checkable against later quarters. Management also raised the full-year outlook on that call, which is one raise on one call and not yet a pattern.

Forward claims we record as claims, not as facts: that around half of RPO converts within 36 months, and that the agentic AI accelerator due in October will compress SaaS deployments from years to months. The test is whether free cash flow follows the revenue.
management.capitalAllocation:
### Capital allocation

Capital is going into capacity, and the cash flow table shows how much. Capital expenditure was {- -$55.7B -} in FY26 against {- -$21.2B -} in FY25 and {- -$6.9B -} in FY24, with FY27 guided to $90 billion-$95 billion.

What that spending displaced sits in the same table. Share repurchases ran -$17.3B in FY22, -$2.5B in FY23, -$3.2B in FY24, -$1.5B in FY25 and -$0.2B in FY26, a descent that was not steady, since FY24 ran above FY23. Dividends paid rose in every year of the series to -$5.8B in FY26, and the board declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.50 per share alongside these results. Buybacks did not stop, they shrank to a fraction of the capital line, and with the At-the-Market program completed in the quarter Oracle is now a net seller of its own stock. The dividend is the shareholder return still running at scale, and it yields 1.33%.

The funding mix is therefore debt, customer prepayment and equity. Total debt reached $156.2B in FY26 from $104.1B, and the prepaid-contract mechanic described above supplies the middle one.

The allocation is coherent and unhedged. Oracle is trading the 79.1% gross margin profile of FY22 for the 65.2% of FY26, financed with leverage, customer money and dilution, in exchange for a far larger revenue base. If FY28E revenue of $131.2B arrives the trade works; if it does not, the debt remains either way.
management.governance:
### Governance

Oracle's proxy was filed on September 26, 2025 and describes fiscal 2025, a year before this quarter.

Directors stand for election annually; there is no staggered board. On the Independence Committee's recommendation the Board found ten of the fiscal 2025 directors independent, and said that if the nominees were elected it would hold five non-independent directors (Mr. Ellison among them) and eight independent ones, as Secretary Panetta and Mr. Parrett did not stand for re-election. That meeting has since been held and nothing here reports its outcome, so today's composition is not readable here.

On pay, the proxy meets the thesis. In fiscal 2025 the Compensation Committee cut the annual performance-based cash bonus for Mr. Ellison and Ms. Catz from $5,207,393 each to $0, notwithstanding actual achievement, and cut those of Mr. Henley, Mr. Levey and Ms. Smith to $0 on the same stated basis, to preserve capital in furtherance of the company's strategic priorities. Neither Mr. Ellison nor Ms. Catz took new equity awards that year.

A board that takes earned cash out of its founder's pay to fund the build is telling a shareholder where the capital program ranks. Set against the capital line above, though, it is a signal rather than a source: it falls on the board's own Executive Chair, for whom it is immaterial beside his stake.
management.insiderOwnership:
### Ownership and related parties

The ownership table is dated September 19, 2025, the annual meeting record date. Mr. Ellison held 1,158,232,353 shares, 40.6% of the class. That share rests on a year-old count and reads high against today's larger one, and further still, because the 6.50% Series D Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock converts into common and can pay its dividends in common too.

Executive officers and directors as a group, 18 persons, held 1,166,800,963 shares, 40.9%. An independent majority is a majority on paper: at that weight the structure above is what a controlling bloc permits, not what a minority compels.

One footnote matters more: 346,000,000 of Mr. Ellison's shares are pledged as collateral to secure certain personal indebtedness, including various lines of credit, under Board and committee oversight. That is a second layer of leverage above the balance sheet's, secured against a stock that has traded from $329.50 to $150.15 inside the year; neither the size of the borrowings nor the collateral terms is disclosed.

The related-person relationships run to Stanford University, where Dr. Boskin is employed and other Board members serve part-time. Oracle's payments came to approximately 0.0002% of its total revenues in fiscal 2025 and, on the company's estimate, 0.0005% of Stanford's in its last fiscal year. At that scale nothing here moves value away from outside holders, and the exposure a minority holder carries sits in the pledging footnote.

idiosyncratic: **Funding ranks first among the risks.** The mechanism is refinancing, not solvency. Oracle spends years ahead of the revenue the spending creates, so it must return to capital markets on acceptable terms in every year of the build, and the coverage ratio in the balance sheet section is the room it has to work with. What we watch is the net cash CapEx line against the guided not more than $70 billion, because that is where the prepayment mechanic holds or fails. Two markers sit behind it: whether the capital step-up ever delivers a fiscal year of positive free cash flow, and whether coverage holds as this debt is refinanced.

**Asset life and residual value.** A GPU fleet is worth what it earns across its life, and the depreciation schedule is an assumption until renewals test it. This quarter the test went Oracle's way, at a 20% premium on a cohort the majority of which is four years or older. One cohort in one quarter, reported by management and not audited here, is thin evidence. A renewal round priced at a discount, or a silence where this disclosure sat, would matter more to us than any single revenue beat.

**Utilization has no headroom.** Management reported GPU utilization of 97.9%. That is efficient, and it also means new demand requires new capacity, and new capacity requires new capital, which is the loop this balance sheet is already inside. The figure is a point-in-time disclosure with no history behind it here, so it cannot yet be read as a trend.

**Margin compression is structural.** Infrastructure revenue carries a cost base that support and license revenue do not, so the more of it Oracle sells the lower the blended gross margin goes. The 10-Q adds supply chain and energy costs, tariffs, inflation and currency as further pressures on this business' margin. The practical consequence is that a revenue beat and a gross margin beat are unlikely to arrive in the same quarter; one delivering both would signal that infrastructure economics are better than we assume.

**The backlog is disclosed in total, not by customer.** Remaining Performance Obligations of $664 billion now have a published level, but no customer concentration figure and no segment operating margins reach us to set beside it. Management named Abilene, a single site where 131,000 GPUs were delivered in the quarter and where six of eight campus buildings, representing 618 megawatts and 75% of total capacity, have been delivered to the customer, in the singular. That implies a large counterparty at that site without quantifying the exposure. Our infrastructure conclusions rest on thinner evidence than our conclusions about the support annuity.
risks.systemic:
### Systemic risk

Oracle's FY27 plan is a levered position on one macro condition: that demand for AI compute stays strong enough, for long enough, to absorb $90 billion-$95 billion of capacity at prices that earn a return. That condition sits outside Oracle's control and outside this filing's disclosure.

Capital markets are the transmission channel. Net debt of $124.9B stands against $54.5B four fiscal years earlier in FY22, and has to be refinanced into whatever credit market exists at the time. No maturity schedule reaches us, so the timing of that exposure cannot be assessed from what is in front of us. Management's description of capital access as an industry constraint is the clearest signal available that this is a sector condition and not an Oracle-specific one.

The 10-Q names the rest directly. It lists inflation, tariffs and trade policy, geopolitical conditions and other macroeconomic factors as influences on customer demand, governmental budgetary constraints as a further one, and foreign currency rate fluctuations as affecting revenues and profitability, which is relevant with EMEA at 24.4% and Asia Pacific at 12.3% of the FY25 geographic mix. Energy cost is named specifically as a pressure on cloud and software margin, which is an input exposure a software-only business did not carry.

body:
### Recommendation

**BUY. Target band $165 to $205, weighted fair value $181.70, last price $150.15.**

Oracle can show both the size of the backlog and the physical work behind it: Remaining Performance Obligations of $664 billion, 850 megawatts of capacity delivered since the end of Q4 at close to full utilization, and a quarter at $19.3B of revenue, {+ +29.6% +}, with the full-year outlook raised alongside it. That is a stronger operating result than 23.2x trailing earnings and roughly 13.6x FY28E EPS of $11.02 reflects.

What still stops us is the cash statement. Capital expenditure was {- -$55.7B -} in FY26, free cash flow was {- -$23.7B -}, the leverage and the coverage the balance sheet carries leave limited room, and the capital guide for this year runs higher again. Until free cash flow turns, the growth is bought and not earned, and the price paid for it is not measurable in any reported figure. That is the whole of our distance from the consensus target, and it is why the bear case argued in the valuation section carries a real weight rather than a formal one.

The backlog-against-cash point at the head of this report is what the band prices: contracted revenue on one side, and on the other a quarter that reported free cash flow of negative $5 billion. What would move us up: net cash CapEx tracking below the guided $70 billion while delivery holds, pulling free cash flow toward breakeven ahead of the fiscal 2028 conversion management describes. What would move us down: a renewal round priced at a discount, capacity delivery slipping against the pace just set, or a capital guide raised again without a revenue guide raised alongside it.
